title: Short Stuff: Fainting At The Sight Of Blood
summary: A Short Stuff episode on fainting at the sight of blood. Josh explains that this is a real physiological faint called vasovagal syncope, tied to a blood-injury-injection (BII) phobia that affects an estimated 3 to 15 percent of people. Unlike most phobias, the heart rate spikes briefly and then drops, reducing blood pressure and blood flow to the brain. The hosts note that disgust plays a larger role than fear in this phobia, and that it may be partly genetic. They discuss an evolutionary theory that fainting could have protected an injured person from bleeding out or made attackers think they were dead. They explain why the condition is hard to study, since sufferers avoid doctors' offices, and note the link to medical procedure anxiety. Finally, they cover cognitive behavioral therapy with applied tension and graded exposure, which can help people stop fainting, and warn that avoiding medical care can harm health.

segments.title: Introduction to fainting at the sight of blood
segments.summary: Josh introduces the topic of fainting at the sight of blood and says it is a real physiological response, not a movie trope. He names the type, vasovagal syncope, and explains the origin of each word part.
topics: fainting at the sight of blood

segments.title: Blood-injury-injection phobia and the fainting mechanism
segments.summary: The hosts describe blood-injury-injection (BII) phobia, which affects an estimated 3 to 15 percent of people and can be triggered by injuries or needles. They explain that fainting follows a brief heart rate spike, then a slowdown that drops blood pressure and brain blood flow. This differs from other phobias, and disgust plays a larger role than fear.

segments.title: Evolutionary theory of fainting and the genetic component
segments.summary: The hosts say the phobia may be partly genetic and ask why it would persist through natural selection. They present a theory using a hypothetical injured ancestor: fainting could make attackers think he was dead, and slower bleeding could help him survive. They admit the cause is still not well understood.

segments.title: Why the condition is hard to study
segments.summary: The hosts explain that estimates vary because people with the phobia avoid clinics and doctors' offices. This avoidance is tied to medical procedure anxiety, which makes the condition hard to document.

segments.title: Treatment with applied tension and exposure therapy
segments.summary: The hosts describe cognitive behavioral therapy for the phobia, led by Swedish psychologist Lars Göritz according to WebMD. Patients learn applied tension to keep their heart rate up and avoid fainting, then undergo graded exposure, moving from imagined blood draws to videos and finally to a therapist with a needle. The hosts say about three to five sessions may help.

segments.title: Health risks of avoiding medical care
segments.summary: The hosts note that fainting can cause injuries such as head trauma or broken arms. They add that avoiding doctors can lead to missed vaccines and cancer screenings, so treatment is worth pursuing.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts exchange a brief closing and Josh signs off the Short Stuff episode, with a production credit to iHeartRadio.
